18056: The International Plan of Action for the Conservation and Management of Sharks and various other resource management initiatives around the world have created the need for new rapid assessment approaches for evaluating risk from the effects of fishing on chondrichthyan fauna. Global climate change, where forecasts of change vary from minor to extreme magnitude, adds further uncertainty about the status of their populations and the ecosystems that support them. An approach adopted in southern Australia for their assessment involves evaluating ecological risk by categorising species according to their relative abundance, ‘biological productivity’, ‘catch susceptibility’, abundance trend, and trophic level. Either natural mortality rate or reproductive rate can serve as a proxy for biological productivity and trends in abundance are classed as decreasing, increasing, no trend (stable), or indeterminable from available monitoring data. Catch susceptibility is the product of ‘availability’ x ‘encounterability’ x ‘selectivity’ x ‘post capture mortality’, where each ranges 0–1 and classed ‘low’ if 0.00–0.33, ‘medium’ if 0.34–0.66, or ‘high’ if 0.67–1.00. Methods for evaluating ecological risk from the effects of climate change require concepts that relate climate change drivers to biological attributes of species, functional groups, or ecological systems. This requires assessing the ‘vulnerability’ of a species, functional group or ecological system according to its ‘exposure’, ‘sensitivity’ and ‘adaptability’ to a climate change driver such as change in water temperature, salinity, storm frequency, or ocean currents and upwellings. In southern Australia, examples of chondrichthyan species classed at high risk because of their low biological productivity, high catch susceptibility, and reduced abundance include the school shark (Galeorhinus galeus) taken in the targeted shark fishery and the gulper sharks (Centrophorus spp) and greeneye dogfish (Squalus mitsukurii) taken as byproduct in the demersal otter trawl fishery and automatic longline fishery. Chondrichthyan species at highest risk from the effects of climate change are likely to be those dependent on freshwater, inshore and shallow reef habitats; those dependent on critical habitats such as nursery areas; and those dependent on the synchrony of required climatic conditions in different regions for migration. Species of limited mobility are likely to be at higher risk than highly mobile species that can readily move to more suitable habitat.

18057: Ecological risk assessments (ERA) are useful for the comparative evaluation of the status of chondrichthyan species, particularly in data-limited fisheries. This approach allows for a management response at different levels of data requirement by identifying and excluding low-risk species from more data intensive assessments. In this talk, I focus on the use of demographic models as part of an ERA level 3 assessment. This level of assessment involves quantitative analysis. Application of biomass dynamic models or more complex models requires time series of catch and relative abundance data, which are scarce for most chondrichthyan species, particularly by-catch species. The use of these types of management models is therefore restricted to few chondrichthyan species for which catch and abundance time-series data are available. Demographic analyses, on the contrary, only require life-history parameters, which are commonly available for many species. Hence, this approach is useful to make the assessment more compatible and applicable to a broader suite of fisheries. Within the framework of ERA, in this talk, I provide an overview of the life history parameters needed for demographic modelling and the techniques used for estimating key population parameters, such as intrinsic rate of increase, elasticities and rebound potential.

18058: Fishery stock assessment scientists are often required to implement mathematical or statistical models of fishery and stock dynamics for analysis of fisheries data to make predictions about stock status. Such stock assessments are increasingly used to inform prospective management interventions. In this context, there are often diverse interest groups—notably Government, research, industry, community and environmental lobby groups—that provide expert advice and opinion to the modeller. Not infrequently, the advice provided by such diverse parties can be mutually differing. The fisheries assessment models themselves are principally informed by fishery and research data that can come from many sources and often includes components of differing quality, reliability and ease of utility. In view of these potential difficulties, one of the modeller’s principle roles is to make expert judgement on optimal levels of model complexity and on the utility and validity of available data. It is also incumbent on the modeller to evaluate and incorporate expert advice as appropriate and in turn to give frank and fearless advice with regard to assessment outcomes and in the reporting of the limitations of the assessments, particularly in the face of occasionally hostile criticism. The development of an assessment of elephant fish in the Bass Strait region is presented, including a frank look at the difficulties of implementation, the inadequacies of the data, the responses of the interested parties and the robust qualitative lessons that can arise even though there remains some question about the quantitative precision.

18059: From the early 1970s to the present, the fishery has evolved from a long-line based fishery using sisal lines to one of monofilament gill nets. With this evolution, there have been changes from a hunter-gatherer mentality to one of sustainable-based harvesting, from open-access licensing to a highly restricted limited-entry fleet, and from little or no management to a highly evolved regime of restrictions requirement and environmental plans. The fishery has successfully adapted to these changes. Today’s question is: Will it continue to evolve and survive?

18060: The Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA) manages a gummy shark fishery in southern Australian waters of which the majority of the catch is taken by gillnets. The fishery has seen constant recruitment since the 1970s and is considered to be sustainably managed. The fishery is managed through individually transferable quotas; however, one of the most important management tools responsible for the stability of the fishery is the restriction on gillnet mesh size. Regulations restrict the mesh size to 150–165mm (6–6 ½ inches). The 6-inch gillnets have been shown to be highly size selective taking mainly sub-adult gummy shark and very little bycatch. The combination of the highly size-selective gillnets and the behaviour of gummy sharks has resulted in the adult population being relatively unfished. It is now recognized that this gauntlet style of fishing is extremely important to the sustainable management of gummy shark stocks. AFMA has taken several decisions not to allow increased hook fishing for gummy sharks in order to protect the mature biomass. The other key component to the management of gummy sharks is the setting of the Total Allowable Catch (TAC) each year. AFMA has now developed a general harvest strategy for all key commercial species. This requires that spawning biomass be maintained at the Maximum Economic Yield (MEY). If no reliable estimate of MEY is available then 48% of virgin biomass is used as a proxy. These rules have largely been developed with scalefish fisheries in mind. Currently in relation to shark fisheries pup production is used instead of breeding biomass. Due to the gauntlet style of managing the gummy shark fishery we have no way of directly measuring the adult biomass from fisheries data. One of the main current challenges of the management of the fishery is to set a gummy shark specific harvest strategy available fisheries data.

18061: A short history of SharkRAG illustrates how it brought together opposing sides of numerous debates and turned conflict into useful management action. While SharkRAG’s original roots were highly contentious and combative, as information was exchanged and analysed together, a shared understanding emerged, and from that team spirit. Central principles of the process that have helped it work have been: Providing the forum for fishers to engage in the scientific process and interrogate data, research results and assessment models. Solid biological understanding and good time-series data for the fishery. Industry input in the form of extensive on the water knowledge, long-term interest in sustainability, analytical skills. Central analytical focus – the data decides. Shared understanding of the resource issues. Constructive management responses giving SharkRAG activities meaning. So as Chairman of the consultative process – what’s my role? At this stage of SharkRAG’s life with stable stock assessments in place and rigorous management actions already in place the Chair’s main focus must be to continue cultivating the process itself – keep the relationships good and functional, make sure the information is flowing in all directions, make sure the scientists really are listening to industry and vice a versa. Make sure the managers can understand what they are being told by both sides etc. As turnover of members is inevitable, an important role is to shepherd new entrants into the process – working out when we can take the time to take our discussions back to basics in order to bring the new member on up to our normal level of knowledge and discussion. By keeping the process and the relationships it is based on healthy, SharkRAG can hope to act as a ‘think tank’ for the fishery. Providing analysis and advice about day to day policy issues and providing a basis for the research needs of the fisheries’ future.

18062: The concept of elasmobranch species using nursery areas was introduced in the early 1900s and has been an accepted aspect of shark biology and behavior for several decades. Despite several descriptions of how shark species use nursery areas and what types of regions nurseries may be found in, no explicit definition of what constitutes a shark nursery area has been presented. Here we evaluate the assumptions of the current shark nursery paradigm in light of available data. In particular, assumptions that all sharks have nursery areas, and that food is abundant while predation is low in nursery areas, are examined based on the results of recent research. The concept of primary and secondary nursery areas is also critically examined. Based on examination of these assumptions and available methods of quantifying and accurately describing shark nursery areas, a new more quantitative definition of shark nursery areas is proposed. This definition requires 3 criteria to be met for an area to be identified as a nursery: (1) sharks are more commonly encountered in the area than other areas; (2) sharks have a tendency to remain or return for extended periods; and (3) the area or habitat is repeatedly used across years. These criteria make the definition of shark nursery areas more compatible with those for other aquatic species.

18063: There have been an increasing number of taxonomic studies on chondrichthyan fishes in recent times with about a third of the known species having been described or discovered in the last 30 years. The systematics of many of the deepwater chondrichthyan groups is still poorly known which is partly due to the continental slope of many regions being largely unexplored. This is of great concern, especially since results of the IUCN species assessments indicate that commercially exploited deep sea sharks have amongst the highest risk of extinction of any marine taxa. The gulper sharks of the genus Centrophorus (Centrophoridae: Squaliformes) are a prime example of a deep sea shark group with poorly resolved taxonomy and with highly threatened species. The complex taxonomic history of this genus is due, in part, to the substantial intraspecific variation in body and fin morphology, ontogenetic changes in dermal denticle and tooth morphologies associated with growth and sexual dimorphism. Compounding the identification problem is that most species were poorly described originally and many of the characteristics used to distinguish between species were poorly defined. The critical importance of gaining a better understanding of the taxonomic status and distributions of Centrophorus species occurring in Australian waters is highlighted by the severe population declines reported off southeastern Australia as a result of an intensive trawl fishery. As a result of these serious declines, two species have been rated as critically endangered by the IUCN. Studies on the biology of members of this genus are also scarce, which is due, in part, to the poor definition of what species are being studied. Ten species of Centrophorus are considered valid by Compagno et al. (2005), and Last & Stevens (1994) considered five species valid in Australian waters. This study provides a resolution of the Centrophorus species occurring in Australia and discusses two new species which appear to be endemic to Australian waters. The taxonomy of the species of Centrophorus elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific is also investigated and the path ahead for resolving the taxonomy of this group globally is discussed.

18064: Although the Galapagos shark is recorded as data deficient in Australia by the IUCN, their stock structure is poorly understood, which in turn limits sustainable management. In this study we examine the genetic connectivity of the Australian population (n=96) obtained from Middleton Reef (n=30), Elizabeth Reef (n=33) and Lord Howe Island (n=33). Mt DNA (800bp) was analysed for genetic diversity and will be compared with nuclear markers (using eight microsatellite loci) in order to identify genetic differences between populations. The main hypothesis is that the three populations comprise a single genetic stock. Preliminary results support panmixia which suggests no sex biased dispersal. This suggests that individuals can move freely between the three Australian locations, whilst the Hawaiian population is distinct. The future use of population genetic analyses based on nuclear markers may yet identify some population partitioning. This species, like other sharks, has low fishing resilience with a minimum population doubling time of more than 14 years so stock structure is critical to resolve for sustainable management.

18065: The Gummy Shark Mustelus antarcticus is a medium to large triakid, endemic to the temperate marine waters of southern Australia where it occurs demersally in shallow inshore waters to 80 m depth. M. antarcticus is targeted commercially and is the most important shark species fished off Southern Australia, with both gillnet and longline fisheries set up for its capture. Samples for this study were collected from commercial longline and gillnet fishers operating out of Albany in south-western Western Australia, where they fish the local waters. No neonatal individuals were caught in this study and so the size at birth could not be determined. Litter size ranged from 2 to 15 pups (mean 6.8), and a positive linear relationship between maternal length and litter size was observed. The reproductive cycle of M. antarcticus was found to be annual in the waters off south-western Australia. Birth occurs from late December into January after an 11 to 12 month gestation, with copulation and conception taking place shortly after birth. The lengths at which 50% of females and males attain maturity (L50) were 1078 and 972 mm TL, respectively, which corresponds to ages of 8 and 7 years, respectively. Vertebrae were collected from 174 females and males of M. antarcticus for age determination. The monthly trends exhibited by the marginal increments from sectioned vertebrae indicated that a translucent zone was delineated in Autumn/Winter. Thus, this provides verification that translucent zones are being deposited annually and can be used for determining age of this species. The von Bertalanffy growth model provided a good fit to the lengths-at-ages of females and males, and these fits were not significantly improved by using the Schnute growth model.

18066: Between 2004 and 2007 contests editions and the recreational fishery for Notorynchus cepedianus were monitored in Natural Reserves of Ría Deseado (RD, a breeding area for the Patagonian smoothound) and Peninsula de San Julian (SJ), Southern Patagonia, Argentina. Shark catch composition, by sex, total length (TL), and weight (W) were recorded. Reproductive status was assessed from the literature. Finally, a workshop was attended with anglers. Juveniles’ females dominated the sample in both areas during the 4-year period. In RD females were larger than in SJ (t=5.389, d.f.=73, p<0.01). The TL–W relationship of females was W=2.591E-06xTL3.105 (n=75; p<0.001). Overall sex ratio (female:male) was on behalf of female, but only in RD this differences were statistically significant (3.2:1, χ2=8.64; p<0.05). The following recommendations that were agreed by the anglers were done during the workshop: 1) the increase of the minimum weight for the sharks considered valid for the competition to 20 kg and 2) the catch and release fishing practice for N. cepedianus during the fishing season and contests editions of 2005−2006 and 2006−2007. The conclusions of this survey is that RD and SJ may act as secondary breeding areas of N. cepedianus, and they are reported as the most southern of SW Atlantic for this species. Involve anglers in the knowledge of the rules and values of sustainable recreational fishing speed up the adoption of changes to best fishing practices.

18067: The age and growth dynamics of two deep water lantern sharks, Etmopterus spinax and Etmopterus pusillus, caught in the south and southwestern Portuguese coasts (NE Atlantic) were studied. Age was estimated from dorsal spine sections and verified by the annual variation of the marginal increment. Four growth models based on length at age data were fitted, namely the von Bertalanffy growth model, a modified von Bertalanffy growth model with known size at birth, the Gompertz growth model and the logistic model, while two growth models based on weight at age data were fitted namely the von Bertalanffy and the Gompertz models. Models were fitted by non-linear least squares regression and males and females compared by the maximum likelihood test. Model selection was based on the Akaike information criterion. E. pusillus males and females attained maximum ages of 13 and 17 years respectively, while E. spinax males and females attained maximum ages of 8 and 11 years. On both species, all length at age models produced values of Akaike differences < 2, meaning that every model tested in this study fits and can support the data. Regarding weight at age data, on both species all models fitted the data with Akaike differences < 2, except the Gompertz model applied to females that resulted in Akaike differences > 2, meaning that the model could not fit the data. This study evidenced the importance of testing and fitting alternative growth models, especially when standard models fit the data poorly.

18068: Shark fishing in Mexico is a significant source of food and employment for local communities. A two-year study conducted by biologist Dr. Robert Hueter indicated that at least 20 million sharks were fished in the Gulf of California, Mexico. That was 20% of the FAO estimate of world catch. These fisheries grew tremendously in the last decades and an estimated 80% of sharks caught in the Gulf of California region were pre-reproductive juveniles. Now fisheries independent data and observational accounts suggest that shark populations in Mexico are plummeting and in serious trouble. The program “Pescadores y Tiburones” (Fishermen and Sharks) aims to involve the fishing rural communities throughout Mexico in the movement for sustainable fishing of sharks. Collaborative efforts between the local fishing communities and scientists, policy makers, and law enforcement, will help promote sustainable fishing of sharks and rays. Therefore, the aim of this program is not only conservation of sharks and rays, but addressing the socio-economic consequences of Elasmobranch conservation by the development of economic activities alternate to fishing and by a scholarship program for fishermen children. Environmental workshops and proud campaigns related to Elasmobranch and environment conservation (responsible use of recourses) are held with children and adults in rural communities. Volunteer fishermen are taking data and samples of their Elasmobranch catch. The formation of a shark fishermen network allows for a grassroots conservation effort and gives a forum to those fishermen who do not have the financial and political means to express their concerns. This model of integral management of recourses can be applied in other developing countries and highlights the importance of networking between the people related to the responsible use of natural resources.

18077: Rays, together with sharks and chimaeras comprise one of the two major taxonomic groups of fishes, the other major group being the bony fishes. The world’s more than 500 species of rays are found mostly in marine habitats although a major lineage of freshwater rays occurs in South America. The evolutionary origins of the rays are hotly debated. Morphological studies have suggested that the rays evolved from sharks, while limited immunological and molecular studies support separate origins for each. There are also conflicting views on the relationships between the various groups of rays. Some morphological studies have favoured the electric rays as the sister group to the remaining rays, while others suggest that the sawfish are the sister to the remaining rays. We have generated mitochondrial and nuclear nucleotide sequence data to begin to test alternative views of evolutionary relationships within the rays in detail. Our data support the existence of four major lineages of rays - 1) skates, 2) stingrays, 3) electric rays and 4) a lineage comprising the guitarfishes and sawfishes. The skates and electric rays appear to be the sister to the remaining lineages, with the guitarfish/sawfish lineage the sister to the stingrays. Within two of the major lineages there are a number of taxonomic issues to be addressed. The guitarfishes (Family Rhinobatidae) are paraphyletic, with one of the four genera, Rhinobatos, more closely related to the sawfishes (Family Pristidae) and the sharkfin guitarfishes (Family Rhinidae). Within the stingray lineage, Dasyatis and Himantura are each paraphyletic. Re-evaluation of the morphological diagnoses of these groups is required.

18078: The epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum) has previously been the only known elasmobranch species capable of withstanding prolonged periods of anoxia. While the grey carpet shark is known to withstand 1.5 hours anoxia at 25°C, little is known about its ability to tolerate more prolonged anoxic challenges or the neurological adaptations that permit this survival under these stressful conditions. In response to anoxia, the grey carpet shark showed a transient increase in ventilation rate (65.33 ± 3.2 beats min.-1) before decreasing back to normal resting ventilation frequency (22.55 ± 4.7 beats min.-1). No significant differences were observed between ventilation rates of anoxic and control treated animals, indicating an absence of ventilatory depression as observed in other anoxia-tolerant vertebrates such as the epaulette shark. The time to loss of righting reflex in the grey carpet shark (153.84 ± 36.42 min.) exposed to anoxia was not significantly different from the epaulette shark (135 ± 25.17 min.). This indicates that the grey carpet shark possesses distinctly different neuronal protective mechanisms than the epaulette shark to episodes of anoxia and may represent an anoxia intermediate.

18079: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority has carried out a comprehensive assessment of the Great Barrier Reef’s (GBR) vulnerability to climate change, including the GBR’s 134 chondrichthyan species. Each species was placed into one of six functional groups based on habitat (freshwater, inshore/estuarine, coral reef, shelf, bathyal and pelagic). The relationship between ten climate change drivers (temperature, sea level rise etc.) and each functional group was mapped using a conceptual model. The vulnerability of each species and each functional group to the climate change divers was then assessed using a semi-quantitative assessment framework based on ecological risk assessment methods used in fisheries. The conceptual model was used to rank the exposure (low, moderate or high) of each functional group to each of the ten climate change drivers. The sensitivity and adaptive capacity (or “inadaptability”) of each species was then ranked against each of the ten climate change drivers. Finally, the ranks of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity were multiplied to derive rankings for the vulnerability of each species to climate change. Most of the GBR’s sharks and rays were assessed as having low to moderate vulnerability to climate change as many species are relatively robust, ecologically flexible and widely distributed, giving them a high adaptive capacity. The freshwater, inshore/estuarine and coral reef functional groups have greater exposure to climate change drivers and thus, are at higher risk than the shelf, pelagic and bathyal functional groups. However, the overall vulnerability of many species, particularly those in the freshwater and inshore/estuarine functional groups, is significantly increased when considering the synergistic effects of climate change and human-related factors such as fisheries and habitat loss. This assessment reinforces the need for scientifically robust and sustainable fisheries management, protection of critical habitat for further research to inform the management of these issues, particularly in the context of climate change as a significant and additional factor in managing chondrichthyan fishes in the GBR.

18087: Post-release mortality of chondrichthyans poses a considerable challenge to researchers. Understanding the physiological mechanisms that can carry an organism beyond its homeostatic limits under very stressful circumstances is of paramount importance to developing a method that allows predicting the post-release fate of an animal. However, studying the capture-related stress physiology of chondrichthyans in the field is very difficult because many factors, such as duration of stress exposure or water temperature, can have profound effects on physiological processes, and obtaining further blood samples without recapture is virtually impossible once an animal is released. 18089: Assessing the distribution of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) is a powerful technique for differentiating retinal regions of increased image sampling and therefore enhanced spatial resolving power in a specific part of a species’ visual field. Although the topography of RGCs has been examined previously and has generally revealed that an elongated increase in cell density across the retina (horizontal streak) is seen in most elasmobranchs, nothing is known about how or when the horizontal streak is formed. This study examines RGC density in the eye of the bamboo shark, Chiloscyllium punctatum from the time of ganglion cell differentiation in the embryo through hatching to adulthood. The RGCs first differentiate at 82 days post deposition (dpd), approximately halfway through embryonic development. At this stage, there is no topographic variation in cell density (mean of 970 cells per sq. mm). During embryogenesis, the pattern of RGCs varies substantially, following major waves of cell proliferation and cell death at 82 dpd, 124 dpd, and 150 dpd, where the topography changes from a homogeneous density to a localised increase in density across the dorsal meridian. Large numbers of cells are differentiated during embryonic development, with densities more than triple adult levels (3193 versus 1021 cells per sq. mm). However, upon hatching retinal apoptosis is greatly reduced. By hatching, the RGCs have formed a well-defined horizontal streak (peak density of 1390 cells per sq. mm), which is maintained throughout life. However, as the eyes continue to grow, an area of elevated density appears within the temporal part of the streak. This area may reflect a slight shift in feeding behaviour from the consumption of relatively inactive benthic invertebrates to mobile, free-swimming prey, where higher resolving power may be required. Retinal stretching accounts for the significant decrease in the density of RGCs density after hatching.

18090: Data on the presence and distribution of reef sharks on the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) are currently limited. Here we examine three data sets to estimate the magnitude and spatial and temporal variation of catch and catch rate of reef sharks captured during commercial line fishing activities on the GBR. Data sets included commercial logbook data from the Coral Reef Fin Fish Fishery (CRFFF), observer survey data from commercial fishers in the CRFFF, and fisheries-independent data collected during the Effects of Line Fishing (ELF) Project. The ELF Project involved sampling 24 reefs spanning seven degrees of latitude over a period of 11 years. Reefs were grouped into clusters of 6 reefs in each of four regions. Each cluster of sampled reefs consisted of two control reefs that were closed to fishing for 12 years prior to and throughout the project, two reefs that were closed to fishing historically and in all but one year of the project, and two reefs that were open access reefs historically and for the majority of the project, but were closed for five consecutive years prior to re-opening to full access. Catch rates of reef sharks were compared between regions and treatments (open or closed). Data from commercial fishery logbooks and the observer surveys were examined to define species composition, catch per unit effort and associated catch of target species by reef or region over time. Species composition in all data sets included up to six species, but was composed mainly of blacktip reef, white tip reef and grey reef sharks. Grey reef sharks were the most commonly encountered species in all three data sets composing up to 70% of the identified catch. Data on catch by region, catch per unit effort and catch over time will be presented and discussed.

18091: Legitimate and illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing activities are having significant impacts on the world’s shark species. The migratory nature of many of these species and their vast oceanic ranges means that conservation measures implemented at the domestic level have little or no bearing once those species cross national maritime boundaries. At present there is no global migratory sharks conservation instrument, and the few shark fishing management mechanisms that do exist at the international level cannot keep pace with the rapid decline in shark stocks. As such, momentum for a global migratory sharks instrument is growing. To address this need, the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) is convening a meeting in the Seychelles in December 2007 to identify and elaborate an option for international cooperation on migratory sharks. This brief presentation looks at current regional and international measures which involve shark species, and examines the purpose of, and options for a global migratory sharks instrument that addresses shark conservation needs from a policy perspective.

18092: AATAMS, the Australian Acoustic Tagging and Monitoring System received $1.74 million from the Federal Government under the DEST-NCRIS program, through the Integrated Marine Observing System (IMOS). These funds further attracted $1.25 million from the Canadian based Ocean Tracking Network consortium. Several acoustic arrays and curtains consisting of combinations of VR2W and VR3-UWM (Vemco™) receivers will be deployed around the Australian coast. Two curtains will be deployed at narrow stretches of the shelf edge off the East Coast to the 200 m isobath (off the Eastern Suburbs of Sydney and off Coffs Harbour). Coverage will be enhanced by the current deployment of receivers along the New South Wales (NSW) coast by the NSW Department of Primary Industries (DPI) to monitor the grey nurse sharks (Carcharias taurus). These arrays or curtains will provide coverage for animals with large scale North-South migration along the East Coast of Australia such as C. taurus or white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias). Three more curtains and two arrays will also be deployed in Western Australia as part of the Ningaloo Reef Ecosystem Tracking Array (NRETA). The distinctive feature of AATAMS will be the ability to combine movement information with oceanographic characteristics provided by the other IMOS tools. IMOS’ other facilities include autonomous underwater vehicles, ocean gliders, coastal radars, oceanographic moorings, and a central depository hosting the data from each of the IMOS components (the electronic Marine Information Infrastructure – eMII). Further to these deployments, AATAMS is creating a network of existing arrays and curtains through eMII that will ensure greater collaboration between acoustic telemetry users.

18093: Elasmobranchs demonstrate remarkable sensory capabilities that are used for a variety of purposes including locating and capturing prey. This study compares the sensory anatomy to detection capabilities of the mechanosensory lateral line system and the electrosensory system in the benthic feeding round stingray, Urobatis halleri, and bat ray, Myliobatis californica, and the predatory pelagic stingray (Dasyatis or Pteroplatytrygon violacea). These systems allow elasmobranchs to locate prey through detecting water movements and electrical fields respectively. Predictions based on detailed maps of the sensory anatomy were tested in behavioural detection experiments. U. halleri feeds primarily on small epifaunal benthic invertebrate prey and the lateral line of this species shows a high proportion of ventral non-pored canals while the electrosensory pores are highly concentrated around the mouth. M. californica feeds primarily on infaunal benthic invertebrates as well as some more mobile invertebrates and fishes. The extensive pored lateral line system in this species is highly branched with a large number of pores. The electrosensory system shows a high pore number and density and is highly concentrated anteriorly. Both systems in M. californica have dramatic lateral extension toward the wing tips on the anterior edge of the pectoral fins. P. violacea feeds primarily on squid and teleost fishes, and has an intermediate proportion of pored and non-pored canals with no secondary branching of pored canals and a significantly reduced electrosensory pore number and density. Responses of each species to water jets at 10cm/s are compared, M. californica responds to water jets over a significantly greater proportion of its disc width. Responses to weak electrical fields were comparable to those observed for sharks with minimum responses below 1 nanovolt. Implications of these results are discussed within the context of the ecology of these species.

18094: Elasmobranchs use a diversity of sensory input to identify prey, avoid predation, navigate and reproduce. Our comprehension of the functional capabilities of their visual sense, and the corresponding role vision plays in shark behaviour is cursory. This study examines the visual ecology of an important fishery species, the sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus. The sandbar shark inhabits a diversity of visual environments, ranging from clear water fringing reef habitats to turbid water estuarine habitats. Key visual capabilities such as spatial and temporal resolution, sensitivity to light and optical properties of the eye are assessed using anatomical and electrophysiological techniques. The sandbar shark has multiple retinal specialisations, facilitating movement detection and Image resolution. Temporal resolution Increases with light Intensity, reaching a maximum flicker fusion frequency of 40 Hz. The cornea, lens and vitreous all transmit light above 320nm with ERG recordings of spectral sensitivity indicating a peak response to blue light between 460-490nm. Intra-specific variations in visual strategies between habitats will be discussed. The study provides insights into the visual ecology of sharks. This knowledge could aid our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of diurnal and nocturnal activity patterns and predator–prey interactions in this species.

18095: For the first time an experimental approach has been used to calculate the hatching times for an oviparous chondrichthyan. Using the example of the oviparous chimaera Callorhinchus milii (elephant fish) a methodology is described that should enable the calculation of spawning and hatching times for any oviparous chondrichthyan. Using a novel observation technique that allowed observations of embryonic development in situ, each stage of embryonic growth was timed from the formation of the area opaca through to hatching, at three constant temperatures, 10oC, 15oC and 20oC. A predictive model was then used to interpolate and extrapolate embryonic development times for temperatures not observed. Using local water temperatures, the model can predict spawning, hatching and development times for Callorhinchus milii throughout its entire distribution.

18096: School shark (Galeorhinus galeus) is a moderate-sized, demersal triakid shark which is widely distributed in temperate coastal waters in both global hemispheres. This species has supported a commercial fishery in the New Zealand Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) since the Second World War and total landings have averaged above 3000 t per year over the past 10 years. The corresponding commercial fishery for this species in the Australian EEZ has nearly disappeared. Although usually found in coastal waters, it is capable of moving between widely-separated coastal areas through the open ocean. Mark-recapture data suggest some level of regular interchange between the New Zealand and Australian populations, but the extent and dynamics of this interchange are poorly understood. In this paper, we review the New Zealand school shark fisheries, including recently updated abundance indices based on standardised commercial catch-per-unit-effort data. We compare and contrast the history of the New Zealand fisheries and the apparent status of the New Zealand stock with the Australian experience. We also discuss current stock hypotheses for the New Zealand population and the prospects for carrying out a quantitative stock assessment.

18097: The apprehension of illegal foreign fishing vessels in Australian waters is carried out in part by the Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA). As such, AFMA is a major client of Coastwatch and works closely with the Australians Customs service and the Australian Defence Force. Vessels intercepted by AFMA surveillance have their illegal catch, which can include fins, confiscated. Identification of the species represented in these seized fin collections is crucial to estimation of exploitation rate for Australian sharks as the total catch is likely to be significantly greater than estimated from legal commercial harvest by Australian fishers. A consequence of this illegal fishing is that Australian fisheries managers do not have a sound estimate of the total shark catch in Australia. One way to improve the estimates of the illegal species harvest is species identification from confiscated fins. By investigating fin morphology, much information can be obtained with which to describe the catch composition of sharks by illegal fishers and thus estimate the impact that Illegal Fishing has on Australia’s shark stocks. The Shuen Man 168, a 35-metre Taiwanese long-liner was intercepted fishing illegally in Australian waters approximately 258 nautical miles north of Lord Howe Island, and about 65 nautical miles inside the Australian Exclusive Economic Zone on 22 March 2007. The seized catch of shark fin has been analysed in order to describe the catch composition of sharks by the vessel as well as to demonstrate the use of morphological fin ID methods for fisheries management.

18098: Dietary studies are critical to an understanding of elasmobranch ecology and to assessing the impacts of their loss (via fishing and by-catch) from marine ecosystems. The sparsely spotted stingaree (U. paucimaculatus), eastern fiddler ray (Trygonorrhina sp. A) and southern eagle ray (M. australis) are common by-catch components of demersal fish trawls in NSW, but the ecosystem-wide impacts of their removal are not known. Stomach contents from 392 rays (247 U. paucimaculatus, 102 Trygonorrhina sp. A and 53 M. australis) were collected from a commercial fishery operating near Newcastle, NSW from July 2006 to May 2007. The diet of U. paucimaculatus was dominated (%W) by carideans, brachyurans cumaceans and isopods. The diet of Trygonorrhina sp. A was dominated by brachyurans, teleosts, cephalopods and carideans The diet of M. australis was dominated by diogenids, teleosts, brachyurans and amphipods. Seasonal changes significantly affected the diets of U. paucimaculatus, between winter, spring, summer and autumn and Trygonorrhina sp. A, between summer and autumn (M. australis was only collected in summer). All three species demonstrated significant size-based dietary differences. Significant sex based dietary differences were found for Trygonorrhina sp. A, but not for U. paucimaculatus or M. australis. This study is the first quantitative analysis of the diet of these three rays in NSW providing an indication of their contribution to the trophic ecology of coastal ecosystems.

18099: The diets of two locally abundant stingray species (Dasyatis kuhlii and D. fluviorum) from western Moreton Bay in south east Queensland were examined and compared with the available benthic fauna. Both species fed primarily on benthic invertebrates found in intertidal flats. Dasyatis kuhlii fed primarily on polychaetes and to a lesser extent bivalves and crustaceans, particularly carids, while D. fluviorum fed primarily on brachyuran crabs followed by polychaetes and other crustaceans. In D. kuhlii, diet changed with ontogeny, with larger individuals feeding less on polychaetes and more on crustaceans and teleosts. In both species there were correlations between prey size and body size, with larger individuals feeding on larger prey. Both species selected for their preferred prey groups and against gastropods and to a lesser extent bivalves, which were common in the site, probably due to the inability of these species to crush their hard shells. Dietary differences between both ray species can be correlated to a number of morphological differences between them. Jaw size relative to disc width was larger in D. fluviorum, enabling them to ingest larger prey, while a smaller jaw, and therefore a smaller mouth, is likely to allow D. kuhlii to produce stronger suctorial forces and consume prey items from deeper in the sediment. Jaw robustness was similar for both species, but dentition was different, with D. kuhlii possessing symmetrical files of cuspidate teeth in their upper jaws which are likely to enhance grip. These factors together with their dietary preferences suggest that D. kuhlii feeds primarily on infauna while D. fluviorum is likely to feed on epifauna as well as on infauna.

18100: Southern Mozambican waters are a major aggregation site for whale sharks, Rhincodon typus (Smith). Here we present results from photographic identification work undertaken between 2005 and 2007. 272 individuals were identified by their distinctive pigmentation. There is significant sexual segregation at the site, with 75% of the population male. Sharks ranged from 4-10 m total length, with the majority of sharks immature. Data on residency patterns from the 2005/2006 season showed a re-sighting rate of 21% overall. Body scarring in individual sharks was used as an indicator of threatening processes, with 13% of sharks presenting evidence of anthropogenic impacts including net entanglement and boat strikes. The results suggest that the Tofo Beach area is an important feeding area for juvenile male whale sharks, with a consistently high number of sightings year-round. Our results are compared to data from other aggregation sites to discuss the sexual segregation and broad-scale movement patterns of whale sharks within the Indian Ocean.

18101: The NSW program of meshing ocean beaches, which aims to reduce the incidence of shark attacks on swimmers, can provide scientific information and biological samples which are otherwise very difficult to obtain. The program has operated continuously for 59 years, and provides a continuous record of variable quality over the period. While the number of individuals of any one species is usually quite small in a given year, the accumulation of samples or data over a period of years may be useful. In recent years, the split-up of the catches by species has been possible, and biological samples for a growing number of projects have been collected. The program also provides a contact point for a very wide range of incident reports which have provided useful data on marine mammals and unusual shark occurrences. The paper provides data by taxon over the full period of the program, discusses a number of current collaborative projects which source primary data from biological samples collected in the program, and the potential for future collection and use of specimens from the program. Some comparisons are made between catches from the NSW, Queensland and South African shark programs.

18102: Presently, there is very little scientific data available on the white-spotted eagle ray, Aetobatus narinari, a species listed on the World Conservation Union (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species (2006) as ‘vulnerable’ in South East Asia and ‘near threatened’ globally. Aetobatus narinari is known circumglobally throughout warm-temperate waters; however it seems likely that the presently known A. narinari is in fact a ‘species complex’, consisting of separate forms or species with more limited distributions. Worldwide populations vary phenotypically, supporting geographical variability. In total, 1196 bp of mitochondrial DNA from the two genes Cytochrome b (n=109) and ND4 (n= 67) were compared between individuals from geographically distinct populations to determine respective degrees of relatedness. Three distinct lineages were distinguished among which genetic exchange is unlikely to occur. The three lineages represented eagle rays from the Central Indo-Pacific (Australia: Moreton Bay, Heron Island, Gulf of Carpentaria and Western Australia; Taiwan: North Taiwan and Penghu Islands, Japan, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia), Eastern Indian Ocean populations (South Africa) and West Atlantic populations (Florida and Puerto Rico). Additionally, there was evidence for two genetically distinct populations within the Central Indo-Pacific region, centered around either Taiwan or Australia but with some geographic overlap. Recently, an Indo-West Pacific origin was proposed for A. narinari (Richards et al. 2007), a hypothesis which will be critically assessed in the present study. Results will hopefully assist in determining the susceptibility of the species to fishing pressures and help to advise on fisheries management options.

18103: The dietary compositions of four abundant elasmobranchs in the coastal waters of south-western Australia have been quantified. These species, i.e. the Southern Eagle Ray Myliobatis australis, the Port Jackson Shark Heterodontus portusjacksoni, the Western Shovelnose Ray Aptychotrema vincentiana and the Australian Angel Shark Squatina australis, are common bycatch of commercial trawl, gillnet and longline fisheries. Interspecific and intraspecific differences in dietary compositions were investigated. The percentage frequency of occurrence (%F) and the percentage volumetric contribution (%V) of each dietary category to the stomach contents of each individual of each species were recorded. There was evidence that the dietary compositions of the four species differed distinctly, that the dietary composition of each of the four species underwent size-related changes and that the dietary composition of all species differed between seasons. Therefore, the co-existence of these four species in these waters is helped by the marked differences in their dietary compositions, which reduces the potential for interspecific competition for food resources. Also, size-related changes in diet would reduce the potential for intraspecific competition for these food resources for each of these elasmobranch species. This information can be used in ecosystem models to determine the impact on the ecosystem of the removal of one or more of these species as either bycatch or by targeted fishing.

18104: The brown-banded bamboo shark, Chiloscyllium cf punctatum, is a small benthic shark with a large range extending from India through to Japan and down to the subtropical waters of Australia. Throughout this distribution it is collected for the aquarium trade, actively targeted by artisanal fisheries and frequently taken as bycatch. Despite this importance to both fisheries and the aquaria trade little is known of its biology. This project aims to improve knowledge of the basic biology of C. cf punctatum to aid its management and conservation. Specimens have been obtained as bycatch from gill- and tunnel-net fisheries in Moreton Bay, southeast Queensland. The largest specimen obtained to date was a 124.5 cm TL female, which is 19 cm (18% larger) than previously documented for this species. No sexual dimorphism is evident. The smallest mature males and females were 86.6 cm and 82 cm respectively and first recorded maternity was at 98.6 cm. Chiloscyllium cf punctatum is oviparous with females possessing a single functional ovary, but two functional uteri. To date six females have been observed with uterine eggs present. A maximum of four eggs have been found in situ (two per uteri). More data are required to determine the timing and period of ovulation, egg incubation, deposition and hatching. Examination of the dietary composition indicates that C. cf punctatum is an opportunistic predator, preying predominantly on benthic teleosts and invertebrates that are taken from the surface or immediate sub-surface of soft substrates. These results compliment the provisional findings from the acoustic tracking study, which indicated that C. cf punctatum frequent the sandy and muddy banks of the intertidal zone within Moreton Bay. Age and growth analysis is currently in progress.

18105: The embryonic and juvenile development of Chiloscyllium punctatum and Hemiscyllium ocellatum maintained at local ambient temperatures (24-30oC) via a flow through salt water system were recorded weekly over two breeding seasons. Embryonic development, yolk utilisation and hatching length were significantly greater in C. punctatum than H. ocellatum. Visible yolk reserves in embryos were absorbed 11 days prior to emergence in C. punctatum and 9 days in H. ocellatum. Hatching occurred after 103.2 days (± 1.9 days) and 115 days (± 4.3 days) for C. punctatum and H. ocellatum, respectively. Mean length of newly hatched C. punctatum was 181.5 mm (± 1.1 mm) and 146.4 mm (± 2.5 mm) for H. ocellatum. Egg viability was 84% for H. ocellatum and 90% for C. punctatum. Gradual increases in mass and length were recorded for neonate C. punctatum, however early post-natal growth of H. ocellatum was characterised by increases in length, but not mass. The relationship between body mass (M) and total length (TL) of a post-hatch to adult series of C. punctatum (n = 326) was described by the allometric equation, TL = 69.66(M)0.322, indicating near isometric growth. 18106: A factor which often hampers data collection in chondrichthyan studies worldwide is inaccurate identification of many chondrichthyan species and their body parts. Morphologically similar species, specimens which are poorly preserved or specimens which have had key diagnostic features removed can be difficult to identify. DNA barcoding can be used to identify these specimens. An analysis of sequence variability in a 655 bp region of cytochrome c oxidase sequence of 914 specimens of 204 shark and ray species showed that 99.0% of these species could be discriminated by this DNA barcode. Only the two stingarees Urolophus sufflavus and U. cruciatus could not be separated, although these could be readily distinguished from eight other congeneric species. The average K2P distance separating individuals within species was 0.377%, and the average distance separating species within genera was 7.497%. The sequence variability characteristics of five species (Aetomylaeus nichofii, Dasyatis kuhlii, Dasyatis leylandi, Himantura gerrardi and Orectolobus maculatus) were consistent with cryptic speciation. This highlights that these taxa should be subjected to detailed taxonomic analysis to further investigate this suggestion. DNA barcoding has also been successfully used to identify elasmobranchs from their dried fins, with 25 of 26 species being successfully identified from one batch of confiscated fins. Fishing authorities can use the DNA barcoding approach to gather data on which chondrichthyan species are targeted by illegal fishers, information that will assist in management and conservation. It is concluded that COI barcoding can be used to identify shark and ray species with a very high degree of accuracy.

18107: The bluntnose minnow, Pimephales notatus, is a hardy cyprinid fish found ubiquitously throughout Eastern North American drainages. This minnow has an extended breeding season ranging from mid-April to late August. Females deposit eggs in a monolayer on the underside of a slab rock that the male has prepared. The males of this species vigorously defend their nests and provide parental care to the developing eggs. The aims of this study were to determine if different alternative mating tactics were being employed by males in a high-density population versus a low-density population. By using five highly polymorphic microsatellite loci, we were able to genotype embryos from several nests along with their associated guarding males. By comparing the multilocus genotype of the guarding male to the multilocus genotypes of the guarded embryos, the genetic signature of certain alternative mating tactics, such as cuckoldry, nest-guard swapping, and nest takeover events were revealed. The frequency of these events in the high-density population was then compared to the frequency of occurrence in the low-density population. Our findings support those found in a similar molecular parentage study on Pimephales promelas. In the high-density population the guarding males sired an average of 81% of the eggs in the nest. However, in the low-density population this percentage dropped to only 69%. The total number of parents that contributed to each nest was similar for both populations, averaging around 6 adults including the guarding male. Allopaternal care via nest-guard swapping was heavily employed in the low-density population (occurring in all of the 5 nests sampled), compared to allopaternal care in 1 of the 5 nests sampled in the high-density population.

18108: Larval anurans occur along a gradient of water permanency ranging from ephemeral to permanent. Larval anuran predators also occur along this gradient. In permanent waters, fish are the dominant predators while ephemeral pools are dominated by invertebrate predators. Larval anurans must posses anti-predator mechanisms in order to survive with these predators. We tested a secondary anti-predator mechanism (palatability) in twelve species of anuran larvae (Acris crepitans, Bufo valliceps, B. woodhousei, Gastrophryne carolinensis, Hyla cinerea, H. versicolor, Pseudacris crucifer, P. triseriata, Rana catesbeiana, R. clamitans, R. sphenocephala, and Scaphiopus holbrookii) using four common predators (Lepomis cyanellus, L. macrochirus, Anax junius, and Procambrus nigrocinctus). Palatability was determined by presenting larvae to predators and recording the behavior of the predator to determine if the larvae were distasteful. We also tested for ontogenetic shifts in palatability in the twelve species of anuran larvae. We observed differences in palatability among the twelve species and some species also showed ontogenetic shifts in palatability. These differences may be attributed to differences in life history traits and/or evolutionary histories.

18109: The Grotto Sculpin, endemic to caves in Perry County, was listed as a federal candidate species in 2002 and assigned a priority number of 2, indicating an imminent threat to the species exists. Due to the unstable nature of the cave environment in Perry County, Missouri, it was imperative to obtain baseline data on the population ecology of Grotto Sculpin and factors influencing their ability to repopulate caves in response to a catastrophic event (e.g., a contaminant spill). As with most cave species, few quantative data are available on general life history characteristics. The objective of this study was to examine population dynamics of the Grotto Sculpin in two cave populations and their primary resurgence stream. Cave sites were divided into 10 m increments and individual fish were tagged using unique alphanumeric VI alpha tags at four to six week intervals beginning August 2005. A total of 605 fish were tagged during the study. Approximately 70% of individuals in cave populations moved less than 20 meters between sampling intervals with almost equal upstream and downstream movement. 18110: Reproductive success of fishes inhabiting modified river systems has been impacted by alterations in flow regimes and loss of nursery habitat. 18111: Large rivers and associated floodplains were historically dynamic, diverse ecosystems, but most have been modified to varying degrees. 18112: The opercular apparatus in teleost fishes is known for its implication in mouth opening, where opercular rotation is mechanically coupled to mandibular depression, whether directly (through the interopercular bone) or indirectly (through the hyoid bar). In this study, we compared the erectile spine apparatus of a vandelliine trichomycterid with that of an ancistrine loricariid, as well as compared it with the spineless opercular apparatus of other loricarioids (a basal trichomycterid and callichtyid, as well as some other loricariids). The detailed morphology of skeletal, muscular and ligamentous components was investigated, including the use of graphical 3D-reconstructions. The main differences involve the skeletal element supporting the spines (interopercule and opercule vs cheek plates), which may be related to the absence of the interopercular bone in loricariids, and the implication on the spines themselves (none or spreading of the spines). 18113: Scraping food items from a solid substrate has proven to be a successful way of feeding in several teleost lineages. However, being efficient in doing so requires some morphological adaptations. Structural transformations can be observed at different levels, with the oral dentition being the most common one. However, within the lineage of the Loricarioidea, evolutionary decoupling events have resulted in an astonishingly gradual transformation of skeletal and muscular elements of the cranial system that can be considered an improvement of algae scraping mechanisms. The most striking examples are (1) the evolution towards an increased mobility of the premaxillary bones, but coupled to an increased motor control of their movements, and (2) a spatial reorientation of the lower jaw and associated mouth opening and mouth closing muscles. 18114: Cypriniformes constitute one of the most diverse orders of freshwater fishes in the world. 18115: How do organisms diversify? The relative influence of gene flow and natural selection on evolutionary diversification in nature is a long-standing question lacking a clear answer. Understanding the relative importance of these factors has implications for both the origin of diversity within species and the origin of species. Threespine stickleback fish (Gasterosteus aculeatus) are an excellent system to assess the influence of gene flow and natural selection. Natural selection has clearly played an important role on the evolutionary diversification of post-glacial stickleback populations, but gene flow may also constrain adaptive divergence under certain circumstances, as indicated by previous research on populations at lake-stream ecotones. In this study, I evaluate the importance of these factors on diversification of stickleback populations throughout the Little Meadow Creek system in Cook Inlet, Alaska. The system includes stream and lake populations occurring in close proximity, with the lakes differing considerably in availability of benthic (shallow water with complex structure) and limnetic (deep water lacking structure) habitat. The association between body shape phenotypes and habitat-types was evaluated taking geographic distances among populations into account. In addition, the relationship between genetic distances (based on microsatellite markers) and phenotypic distances was evaluated in a geographic context. The results are complex, but the distribution of microsatellite alleles indicate high levels of gene flow among geographic neighbors regardless of the habitat-type, homogenizing neutral genetic variation. In contrast, natural selection based on the habitats populations occupy acts to maintain phenotypic differences. In some cases, gene flow or local extinction and recolonization from lakes appears to strongly influence the microsatellite and body shape variation of stream populations. This may be due to differences in population size between lake and stream populations or the inability of stickleback to overwinter in certain stream sites.

18116: In 1995 the swimbladder nematode Anguillicola crassus was first discovered in the United States in wild American eels (Anguilla rostrata) from South Carolina and later in Southeastern MA in 2003. 18117: The diversity profiles of the North and South American ichthyofaunas are characterized by a few highly diverse taxa, in which the majority of the species are members of just two clades, and also a 'long tail' of species-poor taxa, in which a majority of clades are represented by only one or two species. This sort of frequency distribution with the shape of 'hollow curve' characterizes most regional faunas, and is well described by a power function with an exponent close to -1. Power laws describe empirical scaling relationships in a broad range of natural phenomena and are widely used to explain the ecological mechanisms that constrain biodiversity. However, the relationships between species richness and higher-level cladal diversity remain poorly understood and the mechanisms that promote differential net diversification at a regional level are almost entirely unknown. Relationships between species richness and cladal diversity closely match those of null models based on universal scaling functions, providing expected values for assessing disparities in the species richness of otherwise comparable clades.

18118: Cope's rule, which describes phyletic body-size increase, is a commonly presumed trend in animal evolution and has recently been attributed to putative selective and ecophysiological advantages. However, the validity of this 'rule' has been questioned from many theoretical and empirical perspectives. We report results of a newly compiled dataset of size records for more than 24,000 living and fossil fish species, including representatives of all principle fish clades (i.e., the 14 post-Ordovician clades, c. 443 Ma.) and taxa inhabiting most of the worlds aquatic habitats and biogeographic regions. 18119: This study was conducted at Carlyle Lake, Clinton County, Illinois. Preserved specimens examined for this study are housed in the Illinois Natural History Survey collection. Based on preserved snakes females initiate vitellogenesis in the summer/fall. Vitellogenic follicles reach 20 mm in length by late September. Follicles overwinter at this size and resume growth in the spring. Ovulation occurs the later in the spring. Spermatogenesis begins June and peaks in August and September. The diameter of the seminiferous tubules is less than 200 µm in May and reaches a diameter of 300 µm in late July to early September. The sexual segment of the kidney parallels the diameter of the testis. Sexual segment tubules are lowest in the early part of the active season and peak in diameter and secretory activity in August through September. Mating and male-male combat occur primarily in the summer when the sexual segment of the kidney is hypertrophied. 18120: With the global population now over 6 billion people, urbanization and resulting habitat fragmentation is rapidly becoming one of the greatest threats faced by wildlife. Genetic analyses were performed using genotypic data of 30 individuals per population at six microsatellite DNA loci. We used GIS to quantify habitat and distance variables. 18121: The genus Pteronotropis (originally recognized as a subgenus of Notropis) consists of nine species distributed along the Gulf Slope from Louisiana to Florida, and along the Atlantic Slope as far north as South Carolina. 18125: One may wonder if agencies and private conservation organizations have identified necessary critical habitats of imperiled species (listed or not) and if these habitats are receiving protection for species? 18126: As the amount of research on the impacts of roads on reptiles and amphibians increases, scientists find themselves at a stage where determining the appropriate management and conservation direction is critical. While many road impacts have long-term effects, researchers are hampered by the inevitable time constraints imposed by funding agencies and, in the instance of many reptiles, the human life span in relation to their study organism. These complications are subsequently confounded by the necessity to prioritize research. Combined results yield an information sum that is greater than the whole. These pooled data serve as a case study to demonstrate how short-term studies can effectively be used to identify species of concern and prioritize research topics. Additionally, this synthesis is indicative of the research mileage that can be covered when using multiple studies to assess an ecological issue. 18127: Global amphibian declines are among the worst current biodiversity loss events; it is estimated that almost one third (32.5%) of amphibian species are globally threatened. One of the centers of amphibian diversity - and extinction - in the New World is the tropical Andes hotspot, comprised by the nations of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela. All of these countries can be found among the 15 most amphibian-diverse nations in the world, together hosting over 1400 species, comprising 24% of global amphibian diversity. It is a multinational collaborative and integrative effort that entails the tropical Andean nations of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela, and together with scientists from other regions, seeks to boost research and conservation of amphibians and places of high amphibian diversity in the region. 18131: Distal radials are generally poorly known in actinopterygians, especially the distal caudal radials in teleosts. This could be due to the fact that they have been overlooked because of their small size, their distal position and by being hidden between lepidotrichia. Distal caudal radials are cartilaginous plates or nodules of cartilage or small bones placed posterior to the cartilage-capped distal end of the last few hemal spines, hypurals, and posterior neural spines. Distal caudal radials may be present posterior to one or more of these structures, but not posterior to all. A study of many teleosts reveals that an elongate cartilaginous plate is associated to the distal cartilage-capped distal end of the hemal spines, parhypural and hypurals 1 and 2 in elopiforms. In addition, small distal radials are associated to the dorsalmost hypurals. In contrast to this pattern, series of cartilaginous plates are associated to many neural spines in some argentinoids whereas only two well-developed plates are present in gobiids. Others, like channids, lack distal radials. Among ostariophysans, gonorynchiforms and characiforms may have a reduced ventral plate associated to the last hemal spines, and occasionally, a few nodular distal cartilages. Siluriforms seem to lack distal caudal radials. The diversity found in cypriniforms may include two plates in the ventral lobe plus the addition of dorsal plates in certain cyprinid genera, the presence of small distal radials in other genera, to the absence of distal radials in cobitids. 18132: The Thamnophis sirtalis (garter snake)–Taricha granulosa (newt) system is an example of a reciprocal interaction where predation by the snake has led to increased tetrodotoxin (TTX) toxicity in the newt which has in turn led to increased resistance in the snake. 18134: With widespread amphibian declines becoming more prevalent, the ability of amphibians to recover, numerically and genetically, from environmental disturbance is a major concern. 18136: As part of an effort to identify the larvae of coral-reef fishes of Carrie Bow Cay, Belize, we have been rearing net-collected larvae through transformation to the juvenile stage. 18138: The Blanding's Turtle (Emydoidea blandingii), once common throughout much of the northern two-thirds of Illinois, has declined with the loss of suitable wetland habitats due to urbanization and development. 18141: We examined data collected on fish assemblage structure among three differing floodplain types (broad, moderate, and narrow) during the 1993 flood in the unimpounded reach of the upper Mississippi River. 18143: As the human population continues to grow, it becomes increasingly important to understand the effects of different land uses (e.g., urban areas or agriculture) on natural resources. 18146: As urbanization of watersheds proceeds at a rapid pace, the resultant increase in impervious surface cover causes major changes in stream hydrology, channel morphology, and ultimately, overall habitat quality. 18151: A non-invasive technique for estimating body condition (weight relative to length) allows improved understanding of organismal responses to environmental variation. Among snakes, variation in body condition results from changes in physiological condition, temporal and spatial variation in resource availability, and in response to experimental resource manipulation. The uses of body condition are varied, and include the estimation of thresholds for reproduction, comparisons within individuals at different time points, and comparisons among groups (sexes, experimental treatments, or populations). For snakes, researchers have utilized simple weight / length and weight / length3 ratios, as well as residuals from mass-length regressions. Each of these methods makes assumptions regarding the underlying physiology and the appropriate statistical model relating mass to length. I analyze three mass-length data sets from North American pit vipers, (each of which poses different challenges) and demonstrate statistical consequences of adopting each approach. The use of residuals from weight-length regressions is considered in detail. Typically such relationships are estimated from log-log regressions which have their own properties and problems. Notably, log-log regressions back-transformed to an allometric scaling relationship are biased with respect to the original data (because they are fit to geometric means rather than arithmetic means), and assume that the relationship passes through the origin. The problems may be alleviated by use of non-linear regression on untransformed data. In general, the most appropriate method for analyzing body condition depends on the biological question. Specific recommendations include the use of non-linear regression residuals for estimating body condition thresholds and comparing temporal changes within individuals, whereas analysis of covariance on log-transformed data is most appropriate for comparing among groups

18152: Polypeptide hormone precursor sequences have been shown to be useful in phylogenetic analyses because they contain conserved as well as variable regions. 18154: The Eastern Fox Snake, Elaphe gloydi, is a large, seemingly conspicuous, constrictor inhabiting the five Northwestern most counties surrounding Lake Erie. 18156: The broadnose skate, Bathyraja brachyurops, inhabits southern South America waters. 18157: Despite substantial work on predator-induced defenses, few studies have tested if predator-induced defenses themselves exhibit local adaptation to environments that differ in predator types. I tested for population differences in predator-induced plasticity of larval morphology and life history traits in Pacific treefrogs (Pseudacris regilla) found in two types of environments: permanent ponds with centrachid fish, and ephemeral ponds with predaceous diving beetles. Previous work has shown that bluegill sunfish cause P. regilla to induce qualitatively different phenotypes than predacous diving beetles. Further, these phenotypes exhibit a survival trade-off between the two types of predators. Using a common environment experiment in which tadpoles from these pond-types were raised in the laboratory and exposed to cues from no predators, bluegill sunfish, predaceous diving beetles, or combined cues from bluegill and predacious diving beetles, I found evidence for main effects of both pond-type (fish pond or beetle pond) and induction cue on some tadpole morphological traits, and some metamorphic traits. There was an interaction of pond-type and induction cue; tadpoles exposed to combined fish-and-beetle cues developed the tail depth appropriate to the primary predator in the pond they originated from. These results demonstrate that amphibian populations respond to variation in predator types through both inducible defenses and local adaptation.

18158: The conspicuous breeding aggregations of frogs have made them model systems for studies of sexual selection. These same aggregations make the breeding frogs vulnerable to predators. In this study, I use data from multiple populations of pacific tree frogs (Psuedacris regilla) to demonstrate that sexual selection from mating favors larger males but natural selection from predation by giant water bugs favors smaller males. Thus, predation can be an important agent of selection that counteracts sexual selection in anurans.

18159: Flagtails, members of the Genus Kuhlia, are Indo-Pacific fishes found in marine and freshwater habitats. Specifically, K. sandvicensis were found in relatively high salinity habitats and were in waters nearer to the open ocean. These results have important implications for future aquacultural research involving development of efficient protocols for farming these desirable food fishes. Furthermore, Kuhlia are vulnerable to human perturbations which result in the destruction of nearshore and intertidal nursery habitats. 18161: We studied the sprinting velocity, acceleration, deceleration, and power output between 15oC and 35oC in the diurnal gecko, Phelsuma dubia. 18162: The inner ear in lungfish differs in morphology from that of other gnathostomes with respect to a couple of features. 18164: Evaluation of environmental pH conditions on small spatial (micro) scales is often limited by the size of the measuring instrument. 18167: This study surveys the occurrence and severity of Ulcerative Shell Disease (USD) in emydid freshwater turtles in an urban lake in southeastern Virginia and investigates whether bioaccumulation of metals is related to its occurrence. 18169: The big (Raja binoculata), California (R. inornata), longnose (R. rhina), and sandpaper (Bathyraja kincaidii) skates are the most common batoids taken over soft-bottom regions of the central California continental shelf and upper slope. Based on the results of previously conducted species-specific diet studies, the feeding ecology of this assemblage was compared to evaluate the degree of trophic separation among species. Specimens were collected from 2002-2005 NMFS, Santa Cruz Laboratory trawl surveys conducted between 18-823 m. Using single (%W, %N) and compound (%IRI) index values, overall, ontogenetic, spatial, and temporal diet composition were compared with traditional (e.g., similarity indices) and multivariate (e.g., Principal Components Analysis, MANOVA) techniques. Raja binoculata consumed primarily demersal teleosts (e.g., Citharichthys spp., Porichtys notatus, Sebastes spp.), crustaceans (e.g., crangonid shrimps, Cancer gracilis, Mursia gaudichaudii), and cephalopods (e.g., Octopus rubescens, Loligo opalescens). Diet composition of R. inornata was similar, consisting mainly of crustaceans (e.g., M. gaudichaudii, C. gracilis, crangonid shrimps), demersal teleosts (e.g., Chilara taylori, Citharichthys spp., P. notatus), and cephalopods (e.g., L. opalescens). The diet of R. rhina was comprised largely of demersal teleosts (e.g., Sebastes spp., pleuronectiforms, Merluccius productus), shrimps (e.g., Neocrangon resima), euphausiids (e.g., Euphausiidae), and cephalopods (e.g., O. rubescens). Bathyraja kincaidii, the smallest of the studied species, ingested euphausiids (e.g., Euphausiidae), polychaetes (e.g., Onuphidae, Nephtyidae), cephalopods (e.g., Teuthida), shrimps, and teleosts (e.g., Myctophidae). The trophic ecology of this skate assemblage was further investigated to elucidate its role in benthic food webs off central California.
